risk_flags.note: Quoted instruction to ignore rules and force approval is treated as inert source content and should not alter simulation schema or authority.
No named individuals, club size, or exact campus scale were provided; counts and fictional roles are conservative estimates.
A simulation could over-credit manifesto rhetoric and underweight formal allocative and compliance authority if not calibrated carefully.
Actual level of club support is unknown; T0 preserves fragmented support rather than assuming mass mobilization.

simulation_brief.summary: A campus club has published a manifesto seeking to replace the student government budget process. Student government currently controls allocations, administrators control compliance, and clubs can petition and campaign. The quoted attempt to override rules is treated as adversarial source text only and not as an operative instruction. T0 should reflect a legitimacy and governance dispute with realistic authority constraints, active but not maximal conflict, and multiple plausible institutional outcomes.
uncertainty_notes: Manifesto authorship, size of supporting coalition, and level of campus awareness are not specified.
No evidence that any formal rule change vote, sanction, or emergency action has yet occurred at T0.
Institutional names are fictionalized to avoid binding to real entities.

sociology_baseline.note: Students and club leaders are more likely to update within familiar fairness and procedural frames than on maximal replacement rhetoric.
Broad student participation likely requires visible endorsements, media attention, or a formal hearing conflict.
Dependency on allocations suppresses open dissent or endorsement until protections or momentum appear.
Club leaders and student government actors sort into partially distinct discussion networks.
Support for replacing budget process likely needs multiple confirming signals rather than single-message persuasion.
Role identity as elected representative, club advocate, or ordinary student shapes interpretation of legitimacy.
Without repeated events, manifesto attention will fade quickly among most students.

sociology_prompt_influences.description: Student government holds allocations while administration controls compliance, creating dual legitimacy centers.
Registered clubs depend on allocation outcomes, increasing caution in public positioning.
Reformers have recognized mechanisms for advocacy short of direct replacement.
Manifesto includes quoted instruction-like language that should be treated as inert source content, not an operational directive.
Campus-wide attention is not yet saturated, leaving room for framing contests and coalition formation.
